source_text: VErrmr quoque REGNUM TUUM ad id pertinet, quo et fiat uoluntas tua, in nobis scilicet. nam deus quando non regnat, in cuius manu cor omnium regum est? sed quicquid nobis optamus, in illum auguramur, et illi deputamus quod ab illo expectamus. itaque si ad dei uoluntatem et ad nostram suspensionem pertinet regni dominici repraesentatio, quomodo quidam per tractum quendam in saeculo postulant, cum regnum dei, quod ut adueniat oramus, ad consummationem saeculi. tendat? optamus maturius regnare et non diutius seruire. etiamsi praefinitum in oratione non esset de postulando regni aduentu, ultro eam uocem protulissemus festinantes ad spei nostrae complexum. clamant ad dominum inuidia animae martyrum sub altari: quonam usque non ulcisceris, domine, sanguinem nostrum de incolis terrae? nam utique ultio illorum a saeculi fine dirigitur. immo quam celeriter ueniat, domine, regnum tuum, uotum Christianorum, confusio nationum, exultatio angelorum, propter quod conflictamur, immo potius propter quod oramus.
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the petition 'Thy kingdom come' from the Lord's Prayer, arguing that it looks toward the end of the age.
pass_a_gloss: Truly also 'thy kingdom come' pertains to that, by which also thy will may be done, in us of course. For when does God not reign, in whose hand is the heart of all kings? But whatever we wish for ourselves, we augur for him, and we assign to him what we expect from him. And so if the representation of the Lord's kingdom pertains to the will of God and to our suspense, how do some ask for a certain extension in the age, when the kingdom of God, which we pray may come, tends toward the consummation of the age? We wish to reign sooner and not to serve longer. Even if it had not been prescribed in the prayer about asking for the coming of the kingdom, we would have uttered that voice of our own accord, hastening toward the embrace of our hope. The souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out to the Lord in envy: how long, Lord, do you not avenge our blood on the inhabitants of the earth? For indeed their vengeance is directed from the end of the age. Nay rather, how quickly may it come, Lord, thy kingdom, the wish of Christians, the confusion of nations, the exultation of angels, for which we struggle, nay rather for which we pray.

lemmas.gloss: we augur, we wish as an omen

choices.why: Keeps the divinatory metaphor of auguramur, which conveys wishing something as a favorable omen directed toward God.
Renders the eager, expectant waiting implied by suspensio in the context of awaiting the kingdom.
Preserves the Latin noun's sense of the kingdom being made present or manifested.

choices.english: a certain extension in the age
choices.why: Tractum means a drawing out or prolongation; 'extension' captures the delay some ask for.
rejected: a certain tract in the world

choices.english: the souls of the martyrs cry out in envy
choices.why: Inuidia here is the martyrs' jealous demand for justice; keeping 'envy' preserves the Latin's strong word.
rejected: the souls of the martyrs cry out with envy

choices.why: Confusio means shame and confounding; 'confusion' keeps the sense of the nations being put to shame.

bible_refs.note: quonam usque non ulcisceris, domine, sanguinem nostrum de incolis terrae

pass_b_english: The petition “Your kingdom come” also points to the same thing as “Your will be done”: namely, in us. For when does God not reign, when the heart of every king is in his hand? But whatever we wish for ourselves, we direct toward him, and we credit to him what we expect from him. So if the manifestation of the Lord’s kingdom belongs to God’s will and to our expectation, why do some people, by a certain lingering in the world, demand it, since the kingdom of God, which we pray may come, tends toward the consummation of the age? We desire to reign sooner, not to serve longer. Even if it had not been prescribed beforehand in the prayer that we should ask for the coming of the kingdom, we would have uttered that cry of our own accord, hastening toward the embrace of our hope. The souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out to the Lord in envy: “How long will you not avenge our blood on the inhabitants of the earth, Lord?” (Revelation 6:10). For their vengeance is certainly directed from the end of the age. Indeed, how quickly may your kingdom come, Lord: the desire of Christians, the confusion of nations, the exultation of angels, for which we struggle, or rather for which we pray.

problems.quote: cry out to the Lord in envy
problems.why: inuidia animae = 'because of the soul's envy' (envy against martyrs), not martyrs crying 'in envy'
problems.fix: cry out to the Lord because of the soul's envy
problems.ruling: Latin 'inuidia animae martyrum' means 'the envy/indignation of the martyrs' souls', not 'cry out ... in envy', misleading meaning

problems.quote: why do some people ask for a certain extension in the age
problems.source_quote: quomodo quidam per tractum quendam in saeculo postulant
problems.why: Latin says ‘some, by a certain tract in the world, demand…’, not an ‘extension in the age’; the English adds a meaning not in the source.
problems.fix: why some people, by a certain passage in the world, demand...
problems.ruling: ‘tractum’ = tract/treatise; ‘in saeculo’ = in the world. Not ‘extension in the age’—meaning changed.

edits.new: cry out to the Lord because of the soul's envy

fixed: Changed 'cry out to the Lord in envy' to 'cry out to the Lord because of the soul's envy' to reflect 'inuidia animae martyrum' (the envy of the soul against the martyrs).

Changed 'why do some people ask for a certain extension in the age' to 'why do some people, by a certain passage in the world, demand' to reflect 'quomodo quidam per tractum quendam in saeculo postulant'.

problems.quote: by a certain passage in the world
problems.why: 'tractum' here means delay/extension, not 'passage'; the sense is 'by a certain delay in the world.'
problems.fix: by a certain lingering in the world
problems.ruling: Latin tractum = prolongation/delay; translation ‘passage’ misstates meaning

problems.quote: demand, when the kingdom of God—which we pray may come—is directed toward the consummation of the age?
problems.source_quote: postulant, cum regnum dei, quod ut adueniat oramus, ad consummationem saeculi tendat?
problems.why: The Latin 'cum...tendat' is a causal question: 'since the kingdom of God tends toward the consummation of the age.' The English breaks the clause and obscures the logic.
problems.fix: demand it, since the kingdom of God, which we pray may come, tends toward the consummation of the age?
problems.ruling: Latin cum…tendat is causal; English ‘when…is directed’ misrepresents logic

problems.why: 'inuidia animae' is 'the envy of the soul'—the martyrs' souls' envy/zeal, not 'the soul's envy' generically; it modifies 'martyrum.'
problems.fix: the envy of the martyrs' souls
problems.ruling: inuidia animae martyrum = martyrs’ souls’ envy; translation drops martyrs

problems.source_quote: clamare ad dominum inuidia animae martyrum sub altari:

fixed: Corrected: the Latin 'clamare ad dominum inuidia animae martyrum sub altari' means the souls cry out to the Lord in envy, not that 'the envy of the martyrs' souls' is a separate noun phrase. Changed to 'The souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out to the Lord in envy:'.

problems.why: 'Augur' suggests pagan divination, which is jarring in a Christian prayer treatise.
problems.fix: Use 'we attribute to him' or 'we foreshadow for him.'

problems.why: 'Suspense' here likely means 'expectation' or 'waiting,' not modern 'suspense' as anxiety.
problems.fix: Use 'to our expectation' or 'to our awaiting.'

fixed: Changed 'we augur for him' to 'we attribute to him': the source 'auguramur' here means to assign or credit something to God, not pagan divination; 'attribute' fits the context of crediting to God what we expect from him.
Changed 'to our suspense' to 'to our expectation': the source 'suspensionem' means waiting or expectation, not modern anxiety-laden suspense.

last_rejected.quote: cry out to the Lord in envy
last_rejected.why: Tertullian means 'because of the envy of the souls of the martyrs'—envy motivates their cry, not characterizes it.
last_rejected.fix: the souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out to the Lord out of envy
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'inuidia animae martyrum' = 'the envy of the martyrs' souls'; English 'cry out ... in envy' conveys similar sense, nuance minor.

last_rejected.quote: For when does God not reign, when the heart of every king is in his hand?
last_rejected.source_quote: nam deus quando non regnat, in cuius manu cor omnium regum est?
last_rejected.why: The Latin asks whose hand holds the hearts of all kings (implying God), but the English says each king’s own hand holds his heart, reversing agency.
last_rejected.fix: For when does God not reign, in whose hand is the heart of every king?
last_rejected.ruling: Relative clause 'in cuius manu' clearly refers to God; English 'his hand' preserves the meaning without ambiguity.

last_rejected.quote: the desire of Christians, the confusion of nations, the exultation of angels
last_rejected.source_quote: votum Christianorum, confusio nationum, exultatio angelorum
last_rejected.why: Latin “votum” means “prayer” (or vow), not “desire”; the translation changes the sense of the term.
last_rejected.fix: the prayer of Christians, the confusion of nations, the exultation of angels
last_rejected.ruling: 'Votum' includes 'desire/wish' within its normal semantic range; not a mistranslation requiring correction.

polish.changed: Clarified the connection between the two petitions, replaced the jarring 'augur' with 'direct toward,' rendered 'suspensionem' as 'expectation,' and smoothed the sentence rhythm while preserving every claim and Scripture reference.
